Fitted Value Methods

The previous chapter replaced the value function by a parametric function v(⋅;θ)v(\cdot;\theta)v(⋅;θ) and asked which finite set of conditions should determine θ\thetaθ. Its Step 4 solved those conditions by function iteration, a Bellman backup at chosen states followed by a fit, with two particular fits: interpolation at the nodes of a basis, and least squares on a basis. This chapter drops the basis. Any regressor can do the fit, a grid interpolant, a tree ensemble or a neural network, and the result is fitted value iteration. Each iteration is an ordinary regression problem whose targets are Bellman backups, and fitted Q-iteration, NFQ, DQN and NFQCA in the chapters ahead are elaborations of it.

The fit is not free. Value iteration converges because L\BellmanL is a contraction in the sup norm (Proposition 2), and the fishery of the previous chapter showed a fit undoing that. The chapter therefore follows the algorithm with three results. If every fit is accurate to ε\varepsilonε, the errors do not accumulate beyond ε/(1−γ)\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)ε/(1−γ), which is what licenses an arbitrary regressor. Least squares can nonetheless make the errors grow without bound, on a two-state problem whose value function it represents exactly. And two kinds of fit are provably safe: averagers, which include grid interpolation and the tree ensembles of the first fitted Q-iteration algorithm, and least squares weighted by the state distribution of the policy being evaluated. Neural networks belong to neither kind. What keeps neural fitted Q-iteration stable in practice is a set of design choices that the chapter on logged and online data examines. We then turn to the other solver of the previous chapter, Newton’s method, which becomes approximate policy iteration and, for linear features, the LSTD and LSPI algorithms. The chapter closes with the steps that separate fitted value iteration from NFQCA, and the chapter in which each is taken.

One example uses real data. The model with which the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service sets duck-hunting regulations is small enough to solve exactly, so the error bounds can be checked against what actually happens.

Learning Goals

After completing this chapter, you should be able to:

  • Write fitted value iteration for an arbitrary regressor, and recognize collocation and Galerkin projection as two choices of the fitting rule

  • Bound the error of fitted value iteration, and of its greedy policy, by the error of each fit

  • Construct a fitted value iteration that diverges, and state two conditions that prevent divergence: averagers in the sup norm, and on-policy weighting for policy evaluation

  • Explain approximate policy iteration as Newton’s method on the approximate Bellman equation, and LSTD and LSPI as its linear case

  • Name the steps from fitted value iteration to FQI, NFQ and NFQCA, and the chapter in which each is taken

Prerequisites: the weighted-residual template (previous chapter), the contraction and Newton-Kantorovich material of infinite-horizon MDPs, interpolation with cardinal functions in finite-horizon DP.

Fitted Value Iteration¶

Value iteration computes Lvk\Bellman v_kLvk​ at every state and stores the result. With a parametric function we can do neither, but we can do two things that together play the same role. We can evaluate the Bellman operator at finitely many states s1,…,sms_1, \ldots, s_ms1​,…,sm​,

yi=(Lvk)(si)=max⁡a∈Asi{r(si,a)+γ∑s′∈Sp(s′∣si,a) v(s′;θk)},y_i = (\Bellman v_k)(s_i) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_{s_i}} \Big\{ r(s_i,a) + \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} p(s'|s_i,a)\, v(s';\theta_k) \Big\},yi​=(Lvk​)(si​)=a∈Asi​​max​{r(si​,a)+γs′∈S∑​p(s′∣si​,a)v(s′;θk​)},
(1)

and we can choose θk+1\theta_{k+1}θk+1​ so that v(⋅;θk+1)v(\cdot;\theta_{k+1})v(⋅;θk+1​) fits the pairs (si,yi)(s_i, y_i)(si​,yi​). The first step needs the model and the current function. The second is a supervised learning problem that knows nothing about Bellman equations.

Algorithm 1 (Fitted Value Iteration)

Inputs: States {si}i=1m\{s_i\}_{i=1}^m{si​}i=1m​ at which to compute targets, discount factor γ\gammaγ, function class {v(⋅;θ)}\{v(\cdot;\theta)\}{v(⋅;θ)}, fitting procedure fit\mathtt{fit}fit, tolerance ϵ\epsilonϵ

Output: Approximate value function v(⋅;θ)≈v∗v(\cdot;\theta) \approx v^*v(⋅;θ)≈v∗

  1. Initialize θ0\theta_0θ0​ arbitrarily

  2. Set k←0k \leftarrow 0k←0

  3. repeat

  4. \quad for each state sis_isi​ do

  5. \quad\quad Compute target: yi←max⁡a∈Asi{r(si,a)+γ∑s′p(s′∣si,a) v(s′;θk)}y_i \leftarrow \displaystyle\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_{s_i}} \Big\{ r(s_i, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} p(s' \mid s_i, a)\, v(s';\theta_k) \Big\}yi​←a∈Asi​​max​{r(si​,a)+γs′∑​p(s′∣si​,a)v(s′;θk​)}

  6. \quad end for

  7. \quad Fit: θk+1←fit({(si,yi)}i=1m)\theta_{k+1} \leftarrow \mathtt{fit}\big(\{(s_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^m\big)θk+1​←fit({(si​,yi​)}i=1m​)

  8. \quad k←k+1k \leftarrow k+1k←k+1

  9. until ∥v(⋅;θk)−v(⋅;θk−1)∥<ϵ\|v(\cdot;\theta_k) - v(\cdot;\theta_{k-1})\| < \epsilon∥v(⋅;θk​)−v(⋅;θk−1​)∥<ϵ (or maximum iterations reached)

  10. return θk\theta_kθk​

Write P\ProjP for the map that takes a function, through its values at s1,…,sms_1, \ldots, s_ms1​,…,sm​, to the fitted function. Then fitted value iteration is

vk+1=PLvk,v_{k+1} = \Proj \Bellman v_k,vk+1​=PLvk​,
(2)

the projected value iteration (16) of the previous chapter, with P\ProjP now any fitting rule. Two choices define the algorithm: where the targets are computed, and how the function is fitted to them. Nothing depends on the max. Replacing L\BellmanL by the policy evaluation operator Lπ\BellmanPiLπ​ gives fitted policy evaluation, and replacing it by the smooth operator Lβ\mathrm{L}_\betaLβ​ of Regularized Bellman Operators gives fitted smooth value iteration.

The two fits of the previous chapter mark the ends of a range. Collocation computes targets at exactly nnn states, as many as there are basis functions, and interpolates them: P\ProjP is the interpolation operator, and with piecewise-linear cardinal functions on a grid the algorithm is the stationary version of the interpolated backward recursion (16) of the finite-horizon chapter. Galerkin projection computes targets at as many states as the quadrature needs and fits the basis to them by weighted least squares: P\ProjP is the www-orthogonal projection onto the span of the basis, and when the states are sampled from www the fit is an ordinary regression. Collocation computes few targets and matches them exactly; regression computes many and matches them on average. Regression is what scales, because it decouples the number of targets from the number of parameters, and because it applies unchanged to any model that can be fitted to data.

The fishery of A Motivating Example: Harvesting a Fishery Near a Tipping Point ran the collocation version with the hat functions and with Chebyshev polynomials, and its sweep over nnn showed the polynomial diverging for some nnn. The cell below measures what happens to the fitted values at the nodes from one iteration to the next. The maximization over the escapement and the quadrature over the shock are done by the module that produced the figures of the previous chapter.

Source
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

code_directory = Path.cwd() / "code"
if str(code_directory) not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, str(code_directory))
from fishery_tipping_point import Bellman, ChebyshevBasis, HatBasis, solve_exact

bellman = Bellman()                  # backups on a fine grid of escapements, 21 quadrature nodes
exact = solve_exact(bellman)         # reference solution


def collocation(basis, max_iter=2000):
    theta = np.zeros(basis.n)
    steps = []
    for k in range(max_iter):
        v = basis.function(theta)
        targets = bellman.apply(v, basis.nodes)        # t_i = (L v_theta)(s_i)
        new = basis.fit(targets)                       # solve Phi theta = t
        steps.append(np.abs(basis.function(new)(basis.nodes) - v(basis.nodes)).max())
        theta = new
        if steps[-1] < 1e-10 or steps[-1] > 1e8:
            break
    return basis.function(theta), np.array(steps)


print(f"{'basis':<30}{'step 10':>10}{'step 100':>11}{'last step':>11}"
      f"{'iterations':>12}{'rate':>7}{'max error':>11}")
for basis in (HatBasis(12), ChebyshevBasis(12), ChebyshevBasis(10)):
    v, steps = collocation(basis)
    rate = np.median(steps[50:150] / steps[49:149])
    error = np.abs(v(bellman.x) - exact.v).max()
    label = f"{basis.name}, n = {basis.n}"
    print(f"{label:<30}{steps[9]:>10.2e}{steps[99]:>11.2e}{steps[-1]:>11.2e}"
          f"{len(steps):>12}{rate:>7.3f}{error:>11.3g}")
basis                            step 10   step 100  last step  iterations   rate  max error

Piecewise linear, n = 12        9.59e-02   9.45e-04   9.96e-11         413  0.950      0.521

Chebyshev polynomial, n = 12    9.92e-02   8.59e-04   9.63e-11         412  0.950       1.66

Chebyshev polynomial, n = 10    1.07e-01   5.06e+00   1.05e+08         452  1.049   2.79e+09

With 12 coefficients, both bases converge, and the change per iteration shrinks by the factor γ=0.95\gamma = 0.95γ=0.95, as in value iteration. They converge to different fixed points, with errors of about 0.5 and 1.7. With 10 Chebyshev coefficients, the change instead grows by about 5% per iteration, and the coefficients run off to infinity. The Bellman backup still contracts by γ\gammaγ. It is the interpolation step that expands, by a factor of at least 1.049/0.95≈1.101.049/0.95 \approx 1.101.049/0.95≈1.10, enough to undo the contraction. Divergence and Stable Fits explains which fitting rules can do this and which cannot.

Fitting a Neural Network: Fixed Targets and the Semi-Gradient¶

For a model v(⋅;θ)v(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta)v(⋅;θ) that is nonlinear in its parameters, such as a neural network, the fit is

θk+1∈arg⁡min⁡θ∑i=1m(v(si;θ)−yi)2,yi=(Lvk)(si),\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k+1} \in \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \sum_{i=1}^m \big(v(s_i;\boldsymbol{\theta}) - y_i\big)^2, \qquad y_i = (\Bellman v_k)(s_i),θk+1​∈argθmin​i=1∑m​(v(si​;θ)−yi​)2,yi​=(Lvk​)(si​),
(3)

solved by gradient descent. Its first-order condition is again an orthogonality condition, with test functions that move with the parameters:

∑i=1m(v(si;θ)−yi)∂v(si;θ)∂θj=0for all j.\sum_{i=1}^m \big(v(s_i;\boldsymbol{\theta}) - y_i\big) \frac{\partial v(s_i;\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \theta_j} = 0 \quad \text{for all } j.i=1∑m​(v(si​;θ)−yi​)∂θj​∂v(si​;θ)​=0for all j.
(4)

The derivatives ∂v/∂θj\partial v/\partial\theta_j∂v/∂θj​ span the tangent space of the model at the current parameters. For a linear model they are the basis functions, and the condition is the sampled Galerkin condition. The targets yiy_iyi​ are held fixed during the fit, so the gradient differentiates only v(si;θ)v(s_i;\boldsymbol\theta)v(si​;θ) and never the operator. This is the semi-gradient of temporal difference learning. The least-squares criterion of Step 3: Impose nnn Conditions on the Residual, Bellman residual minimization, would instead minimize ∑i(v(si;θ)−(Lv(⋅;θ))(si))2\sum_i \big(v(s_i;\boldsymbol\theta) - (\Bellman v(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta))(s_i)\big)^2∑i​(v(si​;θ)−(Lv(⋅;θ))(si​))2 with the same parameters on both sides. Its test functions, ∂v/∂θj−∂(Lv)/∂θj\partial v/\partial\theta_j - \partial(\Bellman v)/\partial\theta_j∂v/∂θj​−∂(Lv)/∂θj​, form the full gradient, and computing them requires differentiating through the max, by the envelope theorem (Theorem 1), or through the log-sum-exp of the smooth Bellman operator. The two criteria have different solutions. Every algorithm in the chapters ahead, from NFQ to NFQCA, fits to fixed targets, and the chapter on logged and online data studies what happens when the fit is warm-started and stopped after a few gradient steps instead of run to convergence.

Example: A Stopping Problem in Eight Dimensions¶

The fishery has one state variable, and a grid of a few thousand nodes solves it exactly enough to serve as a reference. To see why the choice of fit matters, consider a state with DDD coordinates. An agent watches an index s∈[0,1]Ds \in [0,1]^Ds∈[0,1]D, for instance the prices of DDD assets. Stopping pays the average of the coordinates, sˉ=1D∑ℓsℓ\bar{s} = \frac{1}{D}\sum_\ell s_\ellsˉ=D1​∑ℓ​sℓ​, and ends the problem. Continuing pays nothing, and each coordinate then moves toward a fresh uniform draw, sℓ′=ρsℓ+(1−ρ)ξℓs'_\ell = \rho s_\ell + (1-\rho)\xi_\ellsℓ′​=ρsℓ​+(1−ρ)ξℓ​ with ξℓ∼U[0,1]\xi_\ell \sim U[0,1]ξℓ​∼U[0,1] independent and ρ=0.7\rho = 0.7ρ=0.7. The Bellman equation is

v∗(s)=max⁡{sˉ,  γ E[v∗(ρs+(1−ρ)ξ)]},γ=0.9.v^*(s) = \max\Big\{ \bar{s},\; \gamma\, \mathbb{E}\big[v^*(\rho s + (1-\rho)\xi)\big] \Big\}, \qquad \gamma = 0.9.v∗(s)=max{sˉ,γE[v∗(ρs+(1−ρ)ξ)]},γ=0.9.
(5)

The average sˉ\bar ssˉ is itself a Markov chain, sˉ′=ρsˉ+(1−ρ)ξˉ\bar{s}' = \rho\bar{s} + (1-\rho)\bar{\xi}sˉ′=ρsˉ+(1−ρ)ξˉ​, so v∗v^*v∗ depends on sss only through sˉ\bar ssˉ and can be computed exactly by one-dimensional value iteration. The algorithm does not know this. A grid with 11 nodes per axis has 11D11^D11D nodes: 121 for D=2D = 2D=2, 14,641 for D=4D = 4D=4, and 2.1×1082.1 \times 10^82.1×108 for D=8D = 8D=8, each needing an expectation over a DDD-dimensional successor at every iteration. Fitted value iteration instead computes targets at 2,000 states drawn uniformly from the cube, whatever DDD is, and fits them with an ensemble of extremely randomized trees Ernst et al. (2005) or with a neural network of two hidden layers. All three methods approximate the expectation by the average over the same 32 draws of ξ\xiξ, so they solve the same sample-average problem; the next chapter studies this approximation. The errors are measured against the exact v∗v^*v∗ at 5,000 fresh states.

The grid is the most accurate method while it fits in memory, and it is out of reach at D=8D = 8D=8. The trees and the network use the same 2,000 states in every dimension. The average error of the trees roughly doubles each time DDD doubles, while that of the network stays near 0.01; the figure shows that the network has found the one direction along which the value changes. Both have maximum errors several times their average, at the corners of the cube, where few of the sampled states lie. That gap is a first glimpse of the issue that dominates the analysis below and the batch methods of the chapter on logged and online data: a fit is controlled where there are data, and only there.

Propagation of Fitting Errors¶

Every fit is only approximately right. This section bounds how far from v∗v^*v∗ fitted value iteration ends, and how good the returned policy is.

The finite-horizon chapter answered this for backward recursion with interpolation: with nonnegative weights, the error of the stored values is at most the sum of the interpolation errors of the later stages (Proposition 1). Over an infinite horizon the sum becomes a geometric series.

Theorem 1 (Error of approximate value iteration)

Let v0v_0v0​ be bounded and let the sequence vkv_kvk​ satisfy ∥vk+1−Lvk∥∞≤ε\|v_{k+1} - \Bellman v_k\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon∥vk+1​−Lvk​∥∞​≤ε for every kkk. Then

∥vk−v∗∥∞≤γk∥v0−v∗∥∞+ε1−γ.\|v_k - v^*\|_\infty \leq \gamma^k \|v_0 - v^*\|_\infty + \frac{\varepsilon}{1-\gamma}.∥vk​−v∗∥∞​≤γk∥v0​−v∗∥∞​+1−γε​.
(6)
Proof 1

Since v∗=Lv∗v^* = \Bellman v^*v∗=Lv∗ and L\BellmanL is a γ\gammaγ-contraction,

∥vk+1−v∗∥∞≤∥vk+1−Lvk∥∞+∥Lvk−Lv∗∥∞≤ε+γ∥vk−v∗∥∞.\|v_{k+1} - v^*\|_\infty \leq \|v_{k+1} - \Bellman v_k\|_\infty + \|\Bellman v_k - \Bellman v^*\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon + \gamma \|v_k - v^*\|_\infty.∥vk+1​−v∗∥∞​≤∥vk+1​−Lvk​∥∞​+∥Lvk​−Lv∗∥∞​≤ε+γ∥vk​−v∗∥∞​.
(7)

Unrolling the recursion gives ∥vk−v∗∥∞≤γk∥v0−v∗∥∞+ε(1+γ+⋯+γk−1)\|v_k - v^*\|_\infty \leq \gamma^k\|v_0 - v^*\|_\infty + \varepsilon(1 + \gamma + \cdots + \gamma^{k-1})∥vk​−v∗∥∞​≤γk∥v0​−v∗∥∞​+ε(1+γ+⋯+γk−1).

The value function is an instrument. What we use is the greedy policy, and its loss is bounded by the error of the value function it is greedy for Singh & Yee (1994).

Proposition 1 (Loss of a greedy policy)

If π\piπ is greedy with respect to vvv, that is Lπv=Lv\BellmanPi v = \Bellman vLπ​v=Lv, then

∥v∗−vπ∥∞≤2γ1−γ∥v−v∗∥∞.\|v^* - v_\pi\|_\infty \leq \frac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma}\|v - v^*\|_\infty.∥v∗−vπ​∥∞​≤1−γ2γ​∥v−v∗∥∞​.
(8)
Proof 2

Let π∗\pi^*π∗ be an optimal policy. Then v∗−vπ=Lπ∗v∗−Lπvπv^* - v_\pi = \mathrm{L}_{\pi^*} v^* - \BellmanPi v_\piv∗−vπ​=Lπ∗​v∗−Lπ​vπ​, which we split as

v∗−vπ=(Lπ∗v∗−Lπ∗v)+(Lπ∗v−Lπv)+(Lπv−Lπv∗)+(Lπv∗−Lπvπ).v^* - v_\pi = (\mathrm{L}_{\pi^*} v^* - \mathrm{L}_{\pi^*} v) + (\mathrm{L}_{\pi^*} v - \BellmanPi v) + (\BellmanPi v - \BellmanPi v^*) + (\BellmanPi v^* - \BellmanPi v_\pi).v∗−vπ​=(Lπ∗​v∗−Lπ∗​v)+(Lπ∗​v−Lπ​v)+(Lπ​v−Lπ​v∗)+(Lπ​v∗−Lπ​vπ​).
(9)

The second term is nonpositive because π\piπ is greedy for vvv. The others are γPπ∗(v∗−v)\gamma\mathbf{P}_{\pi^*}(v^* - v)γPπ∗​(v∗−v), γPπ(v−v∗)\gamma\mathbf{P}_\pi(v - v^*)γPπ​(v−v∗) and γPπ(v∗−vπ)\gamma\mathbf{P}_\pi(v^* - v_\pi)γPπ​(v∗−vπ​), and stochastic matrices do not increase the sup norm. Since v∗−vπ≥0v^* - v_\pi \geq 0v∗−vπ​≥0, taking the maximum over states gives ∥v∗−vπ∥∞≤2γ∥v−v∗∥∞+γ∥v∗−vπ∥∞\|v^* - v_\pi\|_\infty \leq 2\gamma\|v - v^*\|_\infty + \gamma\|v^* - v_\pi\|_\infty∥v∗−vπ​∥∞​≤2γ∥v−v∗∥∞​+γ∥v∗−vπ​∥∞​.

Combining the two, the greedy policies of fitted value iteration are eventually within 2γε/(1−γ)22\gamma\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)^22γε/(1−γ)2 of optimal. The bound asks nothing of the fit except accuracy: no linearity, no particular basis, no structure at all. This is what licenses a tree ensemble or a neural network in place of a table. It also says where the difficulty lies, in three places that the rest of this chapter and the next ones take up.

  1. The error is measured in the sup norm, at every state. A regression controls an average error over the states where targets were computed, and nothing at the states it never saw. The analysis of fitted value iteration by Munos (2007) and Munos & Szepesvári (2008) replaces the sup norm by weighted norms. The price is a concentrability coefficient, which measures how far the state distributions that policies reach can be from the distribution of the data. It is the theoretical form of the coverage problem of batch and offline reinforcement learning.

  2. The fit must be achievable. The bound needs some θ\thetaθ with v(⋅;θ)v(\cdot;\theta)v(⋅;θ) close to Lvk\Bellman v_kLvk​ for every vkv_kvk​ the algorithm produces. The function class must therefore be nearly closed under the Bellman operator, not merely able to represent v∗v^*v∗.

  3. The error must stay bounded. The theorem assumes one ε\varepsilonε for all iterations. If the fit error grows with vkv_kvk​, the bound says nothing, and the next section shows that this happens.

Example: Setting Duck-Hunting Regulations¶

The bounds can be tested on a problem that a government agency solves every year. Each summer, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service chooses the duck-hunting regulations for the Mississippi and Central Flyways from four packages: a closed season, or a restrictive, moderate or liberal one, which differ in season length and bag limit. Since 1995 the choice for mallards has come from a policy computed by stochastic dynamic programming, a program called adaptive harvest management Johnson et al. (1997). The state is two numbers from the May survey: the breeding population NNN of midcontinent mallards and the number PPP of ponds in Prairie Canada, both in millions. Ponds follow an autoregressive process driven by the weather. The population responds to ponds and to the harvest under four models. They disagree on whether hunting deaths add to natural deaths or replace them, and on how strongly reproduction falls as the population grows, and the Service weights them by how well each has predicted past surveys. The reward is the harvest, devalued in proportion when the population is expected to fall below the goal of 8.5 million birds, and the season must close below 4.75 million. We take these equations and numbers from the Service’s report for the 2012 season U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (2012) and discount future harvests by γ=0.98\gamma = 0.98γ=0.98. The model module lists the few details that the report leaves open.

The Service solves this problem the way the finite-horizon chapter solved the reservoir: on a grid of states, with interpolation between the nodes. We do the same with steps of 0.1 million birds and ponds, 12,231 nodes, and bilinear interpolation. Bilinear interpolation is an averager, so value iteration on the grid converges (Theorem 2 below), and doubling the step changes the values by less than 0.05. Figure 2 compares the result with the table that the Service published for 2012. The two policies prescribe the same package in 126 of the 150 cells of the table and differ by one package in the others. The published policy reacts more strongly to ponds than ours.

The reference solution lets us check Theorem 1 and Proposition 1 against what actually happens. We run fitted value iteration for 400 iterations with five fits. Three are bilinear interpolation on coarser grids, with steps of 2, 1 and 0.5. The other two are regressors trained, at each iteration, on targets at the same 2,000 states drawn uniformly at random: extra trees, which are averagers, and a network with two hidden layers of 64 units, warm-started from the previous iteration. For each fit we measure ε\varepsilonε, the largest fitting error ∣vk+1(s)−(Lvk)(s)∣|v_{k+1}(s) - (\Bellman v_k)(s)|∣vk+1​(s)−(Lvk​)(s)∣ over the reference grid in the last iterations, and compare both bounds with the value error and the policy loss that we compute against the reference.

Fitted value iteration for 400 iterations with γ = 0.98. The fit error is the largest ∣vk+1−Lvk∣|v_{k+1} - \mathrm{L} v_k|∣vk+1​−Lvk​∣ over the 12,231 states of the reference grid in the last 20 iterations. Value error and policy loss are measured against the reference solution, in millions of birds of discounted harvest; the optimal value ranges from about 30 to 51. Same package is the share of reference states where the greedy policy picks the reference package.

The table supports three observations.

  1. Both bounds hold, and both are loose. The value error is 18 to 118 times smaller than ε/(1−γ)\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)ε/(1−γ), and the policy loss is four to five orders of magnitude below 2γε/(1−γ)22\gamma\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)^22γε/(1−γ)2. The bounds charge every iteration’s error at its worst state and let the errors add up in the same direction for 1/(1−γ)=501/(1-\gamma) = 501/(1−γ)=50 years. Neither happens here.

  2. The policy is much more accurate than the value function. The coarsest grid has 45 nodes and a value error of 2.2 million birds, yet it picks the reference package in 96.5% of the states, and its worst policy loss is 0.10 million birds, about a quarter of a percent of the value. A decision depends on the differences between the values of the packages, and much of the fitting error is shared by all four packages, because their successor states are close.

  3. The regressors do about as well as the coarsest grid. With 2,000 targets per iteration, the trees and the network have fitting errors of 0.76 and 1.47, of the same order as the 0.79 of the 45-node grid. The network’s greedy policy reproduces the reference map (panel (c)): it picks the reference package in 98% of the states and loses at most 0.03. The trees lose more, 0.26 at worst. Their fit is piecewise constant, so it is flat where the value has a slope, and the greedy choice between two packages depends on that slope.

With two state variables the Service’s grid is the right tool, and the regressors bring nothing. They become necessary when the state has many dimensions, as in the eight-dimensional stopping problem, or when there is no model at all to compute targets from, as in the collision-avoidance example of the chapter on logged and online data.

Divergence and Stable Fits¶

A fit that represents the solution exactly can still make value iteration diverge. This section shows how, and which fitting rules rule it out.

A Two-State Counterexample¶

The following example is due to Tsitsiklis & Van Roy (1996). There are two states and one action. State 1 moves to state 2, state 2 stays where it is, and all rewards are zero, so v∗=0v^* = 0v∗=0. The value function is represented with a single feature, v(1;θ)=θv(1;\theta) = \thetav(1;θ)=θ and v(2;θ)=2θv(2;\theta) = 2\thetav(2;θ)=2θ, which contains v∗v^*v∗ at θ=0\theta = 0θ=0. Fitted value iteration computes the targets at both states and fits them by least squares with equal weights. Both targets equal γv(2;θk)=2γθk\gamma v(2;\theta_k) = 2\gamma\theta_kγv(2;θk​)=2γθk​, and the fit minimizes (θ−2γθk)2+(2θ−2γθk)2(\theta - 2\gamma\theta_k)^2 + (2\theta - 2\gamma\theta_k)^2(θ−2γθk​)2+(2θ−2γθk​)2, which gives

θk+1=6γ5θk.\theta_{k+1} = \frac{6\gamma}{5}\theta_k.θk+1​=56γ​θk​.
(10)

For γ>5/6\gamma > 5/6γ>5/6 the iterates diverge from every θ0≠0\theta_0 \neq 0θ0​=0. The Bellman operator shrinks the difference between vkv_kvk​ and v∗v^*v∗ by γ\gammaγ, and the fit then stretches it by 6/56/56/5: the target is the constant 2γθk2\gamma\theta_k2γθk​, and the best line through the origin overshoots it at state 2, where it predicts 125γθk\frac{12}{5}\gamma\theta_k512​γθk​. The fit error grows in proportion to θk\theta_kθk​, which is why Theorem 1 does not apply. Boyan & Moore (1995) observed the same failure with polynomial regression and neural networks on small control problems, at a time when TD-Gammon had made neural value functions look easy.

Averagers: Fits That Cannot Expand¶

The counterexample suggests asking which fitting rules cannot stretch differences between functions. The answer was found independently in computational economics Judd (1992)Judd (1996)McGrattan (1997)Santos & Vigo-Aguiar (1998), economic dynamics Stachurski (2009), and reinforcement learning Gordon (1995)Gordon (1999), and the communities arrived at the same condition under different names.

Definition 1 (Averager)

A linear operator P\ProjP on the space of bounded real-valued functions on S\mathcal{S}S is an averager if it is monotone, that is f≤gf \leq gf≤g pointwise implies Pf≤Pg\Proj f \leq \Proj gPf≤Pg, and preserves constants, P1=1\Proj\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}P1=1. On a finite state space, P\ProjP is an averager exactly when Pv=Wv\Proj v = WvPv=Wv for a stochastic matrix WWW: wij≥0w_{ij} \geq 0wij​≥0 and ∑jwij=1\sum_j w_{ij} = 1∑j​wij​=1 for every row iii.

The name is Gordon’s. The finite-state characterization follows because a linear map is monotone exactly when its matrix has nonnegative entries, and preserves constants exactly when its rows sum to one. An interpolation operator (Pf)(s)=∑jℓj(s)f(sj)(\Proj f)(s) = \sum_j \ell_j(s) f(s_j)(Pf)(s)=∑j​ℓj​(s)f(sj​) with cardinal functions ℓj\ell_jℓj​ is an averager exactly when the weights are nonnegative and sum to one, which is the condition Λ=1\Lambda = 1Λ=1 of the finite-horizon chapter and the property that separated the hat functions from the polynomial in the fishery.

Proposition 2 (Averagers are nonexpansive)

If P\ProjP is an averager, then ∥Pf−Pg∥∞≤∥f−g∥∞\|\Proj f - \Proj g\|_\infty \leq \|f - g\|_\infty∥Pf−Pg∥∞​≤∥f−g∥∞​ for all bounded f,gf, gf,g.

Proof 3

Let M=∥f−g∥∞M = \|f - g\|_\inftyM=∥f−g∥∞​. Then −M≤f(s)−g(s)≤M-M \leq f(s) - g(s) \leq M−M≤f(s)−g(s)≤M for all sss, which can be written as g−M1≤f≤g+M1g - M\mathbf{1} \leq f \leq g + M\mathbf{1}g−M1≤f≤g+M1. By monotonicity, P(g−M1)≤Pf≤P(g+M1)\Proj(g - M\mathbf{1}) \leq \Proj f \leq \Proj(g + M\mathbf{1})P(g−M1)≤Pf≤P(g+M1). By linearity and constant preservation, Pg−M1≤Pf≤Pg+M1\Proj g - M\mathbf{1} \leq \Proj f \leq \Proj g + M\mathbf{1}Pg−M1≤Pf≤Pg+M1, which means ∣Pf(s)−Pg(s)∣≤M|\Proj f(s) - \Proj g(s)| \leq M∣Pf(s)−Pg(s)∣≤M for all sss.

An averager acts like a weighted average: it respects order and cannot amplify differences. The least-squares fit of the counterexample is not one. It maps the constant function (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1) to (3/5,6/5)(3/5, 6/5)(3/5,6/5), so it does not preserve constants, and it does not respect order either. Polynomial interpolation at Chebyshev nodes preserves constants but is not monotone: its cardinal functions dip below zero between the nodes, and its Lebesgue constant is about 2.4 for ten nodes. That is how the ten-coefficient polynomial of the fishery (Fitted Value Iteration) could undo the contraction of the Bellman backup, while the hat functions, whose cardinal functions are nonnegative, could not.

Theorem 2 (Fitted value iteration with an averager converges)

Let L\BellmanL be a γ\gammaγ-contraction in the sup norm on the bounded functions on S\mathcal{S}S, and let P\ProjP be an averager. Then PL\Proj \BellmanPL is a γ\gammaγ-contraction, so fitted value iteration vk+1=PLvkv_{k+1} = \Proj \Bellman v_kvk+1​=PLvk​ converges from any v0v_0v0​ to the unique fixed point vP∈Range(P)v_\Proj \in \text{Range}(\Proj)vP​∈Range(P), and

∥vP−v∗∥∞≤11−γ∥Pv∗−v∗∥∞.\|v_\Proj - v^*\|_\infty \leq \frac{1}{1-\gamma} \|\Proj v^* - v^*\|_\infty .∥vP​−v∗∥∞​≤1−γ1​∥Pv∗−v∗∥∞​.
(11)
Proof 4

By Proposition 2, P\ProjP is nonexpansive. Since L\BellmanL is a γ\gammaγ-contraction,

∥PLf−PLg∥∞≤∥Lf−Lg∥∞≤γ∥f−g∥∞,\|\Proj \Bellman f - \Proj \Bellman g\|_\infty \leq \|\Bellman f - \Bellman g\|_\infty \leq \gamma\|f-g\|_\infty,∥PLf−PLg∥∞​≤∥Lf−Lg∥∞​≤γ∥f−g∥∞​,
(12)

so PL\Proj \BellmanPL is a γ\gammaγ-contraction and Theorem 3 gives the unique fixed point and global convergence. For the error bound, use vP=PLvPv_\Proj = \Proj\Bellman v_\ProjvP​=PLvP​ and v∗=Lv∗v^* = \Bellman v^*v∗=Lv∗:

∥vP−v∗∥∞≤∥PLvP−PLv∗∥∞+∥PLv∗−v∗∥∞≤γ∥vP−v∗∥∞+∥Pv∗−v∗∥∞,\|v_\Proj - v^*\|_\infty \leq \|\Proj\Bellman v_\Proj - \Proj\Bellman v^*\|_\infty + \|\Proj \Bellman v^* - v^*\|_\infty \leq \gamma \|v_\Proj - v^*\|_\infty + \|\Proj v^* - v^*\|_\infty,∥vP​−v∗∥∞​≤∥PLvP​−PLv∗∥∞​+∥PLv∗−v∗∥∞​≤γ∥vP​−v∗∥∞​+∥Pv∗−v∗∥∞​,
(13)

and rearranging gives the claim.

The theorem is due to Santos & Vigo-Aguiar (1998) for monotone approximation operators and to Gordon (1995) for averagers; the proof of the proposition follows Stachurski (2009). The fixed-point error is the best-approximation error ∥Pv∗−v∗∥∞\|\Proj v^* - v^*\|_\infty∥Pv∗−v∗∥∞​ amplified by (1−γ)−1(1-\gamma)^{-1}(1−γ)−1. For an averager the per-iteration error stays bounded, so the result is the special case of Theorem 1 in which the third difficulty above cannot arise.

The stochastic matrix gives the averaging a Markov-chain reading: Pv\Proj vPv is an expected value after one random transition, and expectations preserve order. The finite-horizon chapter made the same observation about linear interpolation, which replaces a deterministic successor by a random grid node with the interpolation weights as probabilities. Composing that chain with the model’s own transitions makes PL\Proj\BellmanPL the Bellman operator of a finite-state MDP, which is why it contracts.

Which regressors are averagers? State aggregation, kkk-nearest neighbors, kernel smoothing with nonnegative kernels normalized to sum to one, and multilinear interpolation on a grid all predict a convex combination of training targets whose weights depend only on the states. So does a regression tree, which predicts the average of the targets in a leaf, as long as its partition of the state space does not depend on the targets. Ernst et al. (2005) used this to give tree-based fitted Q-iteration a convergence guarantee. Their extremely randomized trees choose splits with the help of the targets, and freezing the tree structure after some iterations restores the guarantee. Linear least squares, high-order polynomial interpolation, and neural networks are not averagers.

MethodAverager?Notes
Piecewise linear interpolationYesBarycentric weights are nonnegative and sum to one
Multilinear interpolation (grid)YesWeights are products of one-dimensional hat functions
Shape-preserving splines (Schumaker)YesDesigned to maintain monotonicity
State aggregation, kkk-nearest neighborsYesEqual weights within a group or neighborhood
Kernel smoothing (nonnegative kernels)YesIf the weights are normalized to sum to one
Regression trees and forests, fixed partitionYesLeaf averages; guarantee lost if splits depend on the targets
High-order polynomial interpolationNoNegative weights (Runge phenomenon)
Least squares on an arbitrary basisNoThe counterexample above
Neural networksNoNo sign or normalization constraint on the fit

The table puts the fits of the two chapters in their place. Collocation with piecewise-linear interpolation is an averager, and the folk wisdom that linear interpolation is safe for value iteration is a theorem. Collocation with a high-order polynomial is not, and its convergence in the fishery, when it happened, was not guaranteed. Galerkin projection and least squares are not averagers. The tree ensemble of the eight-dimensional example sits on the boundary, and the network is outside. The solver matters too: Newton’s method never iterates PL\Proj\BellmanPL, so it does not need the contraction, which is why the hybrid strategy of Step 4: Solve the nnn Equations starts with a monotone, low-order fit and switches to Newton with the accurate one.

Exercises: Divergence and Averagers

  1. The counterexample with an averager. Replace the least-squares fit in the two-state example by state aggregation into a single group. Write P\ProjP as a matrix, check that it is an averager, and show that fitted value iteration converges for every γ<1\gamma < 1γ<1. What is its fixed point?

  2. A non-monotone example. Using Lagrange interpolation with 4 equally spaced nodes on [0,1][0, 1][0,1], compute the interpolation weights for the point x=0.1x = 0.1x=0.1. Show that some weights are negative.

  3. Verifying monotonicity. Consider piecewise linear interpolation on a 5-point grid. Write out the interpolation weights for a point between grid points 2 and 3. Verify that all weights are nonnegative and sum to one.

  4. Trees. Show that a regression tree with a fixed partition is an averager. Explain why a tree that chooses its splits by the targets can change its partition from one iteration to the next, and which step of the proof of Theorem 2 this breaks.

On-Policy Weighting Rescues Policy Evaluation¶

The counterexample has a second reading. The chain moves from state 1 to state 2 and stays there, so its stationary distribution puts all its mass on state 2. If the fit weights each state by that distribution, it minimizes (2θ−2γθk)2(2\theta - 2\gamma\theta_k)^2(2θ−2γθk​)2 alone, and θk+1=γθk\theta_{k+1} = \gamma\theta_kθk+1​=γθk​ converges. The equal weighting was the problem: it gives the state that the process leaves at once the same weight as the state where it stays.

This observation is a theorem for policy evaluation Tsitsiklis & Van Roy (1997), proved to explain the convergence of TD(0) with linear features. Take a finite state space S={s1,…,sm}\mathcal{S} = \{s_1,\ldots,s_m\}S={s1​,…,sm​}, a feature matrix Φ∈Rm×n\boldsymbol{\Phi} \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}Φ∈Rm×n with rows φ(s)⊤\boldsymbol\varphi(s)^\topφ(s)⊤, and a distribution ξ\xiξ over states with Ξ=diag(ξ)\boldsymbol{\Xi} = \text{diag}(\xi)Ξ=diag(ξ). The ξ\xiξ-weighted inner product, norm, and least-squares projection onto the span of the features are

⟨u,v⟩ξ=u⊤Ξv,∥v∥ξ=v⊤Ξv,P=Φ(Φ⊤ΞΦ)−1Φ⊤Ξ.\langle u, v \rangle_\xi = u^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} v, \qquad \|v\|_\xi = \sqrt{v^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} v}, \qquad \Proj = \boldsymbol{\Phi}(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} \boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1} \boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi}.⟨u,v⟩ξ​=u⊤Ξv,∥v∥ξ​=v⊤Ξv​,P=Φ(Φ⊤ΞΦ)−1Φ⊤Ξ.
(14)

In reinforcement learning the weighting is not a free choice: the states in the data are those the process visits, and if the chain under π\piπ is ergodic their distribution approaches the stationary distribution ξ\xiξ with ξ⊤Pπ=ξ⊤\xi^\top\mathbf{P}_\pi = \xi^\topξ⊤Pπ​=ξ⊤. Suppose that is the weighting. We show that P\ProjP is nonexpansive and Lπ\BellmanPiLπ​ is a γ\gammaγ-contraction, both in ∥⋅∥ξ\|\cdot\|_\xi∥⋅∥ξ​, so that

∥PLπv−PLπw∥ξ≤∥Lπv−Lπw∥ξ≤γ∥v−w∥ξ.\|\Proj \BellmanPi v - \Proj \BellmanPi w\|_\xi \leq \|\BellmanPi v - \BellmanPi w\|_\xi \leq \gamma \|v - w\|_\xi.∥PLπ​v−PLπ​w∥ξ​≤∥Lπ​v−Lπ​w∥ξ​≤γ∥v−w∥ξ​.

Convergence came from matching the weighting to the operator, not from any property of the fit beyond orthogonality: ξ\xiξ must be the stationary distribution of the very Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​ that appears in Lπ\BellmanPiLπ​. When the data are collected by following π\piπ, this holds automatically, which is on-policy learning. When they come from another behavior policy, as in the counterexample’s equal weighting or in learning from a replay buffer filled by older policies, the Jensen step fails, Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​ need not be nonexpansive in ∥⋅∥ξ\|\cdot\|_\xi∥⋅∥ξ​, and PLπ\Proj\BellmanPiPLπ​ may not contract. Baird’s counterexample Baird (1995) is the classical demonstration.

The Optimality Operator and the Deadly Triad¶

The weighted argument does not extend to the optimality operator Lv=max⁡a[ra+γPav]\Bellman v = \max_a [\mathbf{r}_a + \gamma \mathbf{P}_a v]Lv=maxa​[ra​+γPa​v]. The obstacle is the Jensen step. For the optimality operator we would need to bound [max⁡a∑s′p(s′∣s,a)z(s′)]2\big[\max_{a} \sum_{s'} p(s'|s,a) z(s')\big]^2[maxa​∑s′​p(s′∣s,a)z(s′)]2, and a maximum of averages is not an average. Nor is there a single stationary distribution to match, since the greedy policy, and with it the state distribution, changes from iteration to iteration.

Sutton & Barto (2018) call the combination of function approximation, bootstrapping (targets built from the current estimate), and off-policy data the deadly triad: any two are manageable, all three can diverge. Fitted Q-iteration with a neural network has all three. There is no general convergence theorem for it, and divergence can be observed on small examples. Yet NFQ and DQN solve many problems, because of design choices that limit the damage: each fit is run against targets held fixed, the fit is warm-started from the previous parameters, a separate target network changes slowly, and a large replay buffer keeps the data distribution from tracking every change of policy. The chapter on logged and online data examines these choices one by one.

Approximate Policy Iteration¶

In the exact setting, Newton’s method on the Bellman equation is policy iteration (Newton-Kantorovich and Policy Iteration): by the envelope theorem the Jacobian at vkv_kvk​ involves the transition matrix of the greedy policy πk\pi_kπk​, and the Newton step solves the evaluation equation of πk\pi_kπk​. The previous chapter showed the same for collocation, where the Newton step (21) is the evaluation equation of πk\pi_kπk​ imposed at the nodes and solved within the span of the basis. With an arbitrary parametric value function the pattern is the same, except that the evaluation is done within the function class by whatever means are available. The algorithm alternates approximate evaluation, finding θ\thetaθ with v(⋅;θ)≈vπkv(\cdot;\theta) \approx v_{\pi_k}v(⋅;θ)≈vπk​​, and greedy improvement. This is approximate policy iteration. Its guarantee has the same form as for fitted value iteration: if every evaluation is accurate to ε\varepsilonε in the sup norm, the policies are eventually within 2γε/(1−γ)22\gamma\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)^22γε/(1−γ)2 of optimal Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis (1996). Unlike exact policy iteration, the sequence of policies need not improve monotonically, and it can cycle among a few policies. With the smooth Bellman operator, the Jacobian is γPπk\gamma\mathbf{P}_{\pi_k}γPπk​​ for the softmax policy, with no ties to resolve (Smooth Policy Iteration Is Newton’s Method).

The Linear Case: LSTD and LSPI¶

When the features enter linearly and the state space is finite, the approximate evaluation step has a closed form. The fixed point of fitted policy evaluation solves the projected Bellman equation (18). Its residual Lπv−v\BellmanPi v - vLπ​v−v is ξ\xiξ-orthogonal to every feature, which in matrix form reads

Φ⊤Ξ(rπ+γPπΦθ−Φθ)=0,that isΦ⊤Ξ(Φ−γPπΦ)θ=Φ⊤Ξrπ.\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} (\mathbf{r}_\pi + \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi \boldsymbol{\Phi} \theta - \boldsymbol{\Phi} \theta) = \mathbf{0}, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} (\boldsymbol{\Phi} - \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi \boldsymbol{\Phi}) \theta = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} \mathbf{r}_\pi.Φ⊤Ξ(rπ​+γPπ​Φθ−Φθ)=0,that isΦ⊤Ξ(Φ−γPπ​Φ)θ=Φ⊤Ξrπ​.
(19)

This is the LSTD (least-squares temporal difference) solution of Bradtke & Barto (1996), an n×nn\times nn×n linear system Aθ=b\mathbf{A}\theta = \mathbf{b}Aθ=b, and the Galerkin counterpart of the collocation step (21). The practical algorithm never forms Φ\boldsymbol\PhiΦ over all states or Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​ explicitly. It accumulates A=Es∼ξ[φ(s)(φ(s)−γφ(s′))⊤]\mathbf{A} = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \xi}[\boldsymbol{\varphi}(s)(\boldsymbol{\varphi}(s) - \gamma \boldsymbol{\varphi}(s'))^\top]A=Es∼ξ​[φ(s)(φ(s)−γφ(s′))⊤] and b=Es∼ξ[φ(s)r]\mathbf{b} = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \xi}[\boldsymbol{\varphi}(s) r]b=Es∼ξ​[φ(s)r] from sampled transitions (s,r,s′)(s, r, s')(s,r,s′), which is possible because the system is linear in the unknown. On a 3-state chain under a fixed policy, with Pπ=(0.70.20.10.30.40.30.10.30.6)\mathbf{P}_\pi = \begin{pmatrix} 0.7 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & 0.4 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.3 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}Pπ​=⎝⎛​0.70.30.1​0.20.40.3​0.10.30.6​⎠⎞​, rπ=(1,2,0)\mathbf{r}_\pi = (1, 2, 0)rπ​=(1,2,0), features φ(s)=(1,s)\varphi(s) = (1, s)φ(s)=(1,s) and uniform weights:

Source
import numpy as np

P_pi = np.array([[0.7, 0.2, 0.1], [0.3, 0.4, 0.3], [0.1, 0.3, 0.6]])
r_pi = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 0.0])
gamma = 0.9

# Feature matrix: phi_1(s) = 1, phi_2(s) = s
states = np.array([1, 2, 3])
Phi = np.column_stack([np.ones(3), states])

# Uniform weighting
xi = np.ones(3) / 3
Xi = np.diag(xi)

# LSTD matrices
A = Phi.T @ Xi @ (Phi - gamma * P_pi @ Phi)
b = Phi.T @ Xi @ r_pi

theta_lstd = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
v_lstd = Phi @ theta_lstd
v_exact = np.linalg.solve(np.eye(3) - gamma * P_pi, r_pi)

print(f"LSTD solution: theta = ({theta_lstd[0]:.4f}, {theta_lstd[1]:.4f})")
print(f"\n{'State':<8} {'Exact':<12} {'LSTD':<12} {'Error':<12}")
print("-" * 44)
for s in range(3):
    print(f"{s+1:<8} {v_exact[s]:<12.4f} {v_lstd[s]:<12.4f} {v_lstd[s] - v_exact[s]:<12.4f}")

# Verify orthogonality
residual = r_pi + gamma * P_pi @ v_lstd - v_lstd
print(f"\nGalerkin orthogonality: <residual, phi_1> = {np.sum(xi * residual * Phi[:,0]):.6f}")

With the max back in, Newton’s method on the projected optimality equation Φ⊤Ξ(L(Φθ)−Φθ)=0\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi}\big(\Bellman(\boldsymbol\Phi\theta) - \boldsymbol{\Phi} \theta\big) = \mathbf{0}Φ⊤Ξ(L(Φθ)−Φθ)=0 uses the envelope-theorem Jacobian Φ⊤Ξ(γPπkΦ−Φ)\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} (\gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_k} \boldsymbol{\Phi} - \boldsymbol{\Phi})Φ⊤Ξ(γPπk​​Φ−Φ) at the greedy policy πk\pi_kπk​, and the Newton step is

Φ⊤Ξ(Φ−γPπkΦ) θ(k+1)=Φ⊤Ξrπk,\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} (\boldsymbol{\Phi} - \gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_k} \boldsymbol{\Phi})\, \theta^{(k+1)} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} \mathbf{r}_{\pi_k},Φ⊤Ξ(Φ−γPπk​​Φ)θ(k+1)=Φ⊤Ξrπk​​,
(20)

the LSTD system for πk\pi_kπk​. Alternating greedy improvement with LSTD evaluation is LSPI (least-squares policy iteration) Lagoudakis & Parr (2003). Compare it with fitted value iteration in the same coordinates, Φ⊤ΞΦ θ(k+1)=Φ⊤Ξ(rπk+γPπkΦθ(k))\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} \boldsymbol{\Phi}\, \theta^{(k+1)} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} (\mathbf{r}_{\pi_k} + \gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_k} \boldsymbol{\Phi} \theta^{(k)})Φ⊤ΞΦθ(k+1)=Φ⊤Ξ(rπk​​+γPπk​​Φθ(k)): both use the greedy policy, but fitted value iteration applies its Bellman operator once and regresses, while LSPI solves for its value.

The closed forms need the features to enter linearly, and linear features are rarely what practice uses. With a neural network the evaluation step has no closed form, and the natural replacement is a few sweeps of fitted policy evaluation, q←PLπqq \leftarrow \Proj\BellmanPi qq←PLπ​q, which is what the critic of NFQCA does.

Exercises: LSTD and LSPI

  1. Computing the stationary distribution. For the 3-state chain above, compute the stationary distribution ξ\xiξ satisfying ξ⊤Pπ=ξ⊤\xi^\top \mathbf{P}_\pi = \xi^\topξ⊤Pπ​=ξ⊤.

  2. LSTD with stationary weighting. Recompute the LSTD solution using the stationary distribution instead of uniform weighting. Compare the approximation error.

  3. Two updates. On a small MDP with two actions and linear features, implement fitted value iteration and LSPI (20). Compare the number of iterations, and find features under which LSPI cycles between two policies.

From Fitted Value Iteration to FQI and NFQCA¶

Fitted value iteration, as stated here, assumes four things that NFQCA does not, and each of the next chapters removes one of them.

First, it learns values of states. To act greedily with respect to v(⋅;θ)v(\cdot;\theta)v(⋅;θ) requires, at every decision, the expectation r(s,a)+γ E[v(s′;θ)∣s,a]r(s,a) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}[v(s';\theta) \mid s,a]r(s,a)+γE[v(s′;θ)∣s,a] for every action: the model and an integral at decision time. The chapter on sampled Bellman updates moves that work into training by learning the value of each action, q(s,a;θ)q(s,a;\theta)q(s,a;θ), so that acting is a maximization over the stored values and needs no model. The Bellman operator on action values is again a γ\gammaγ-contraction, and everything in this chapter applies to it unchanged. Fitted value iteration on qqq is fitted Q-iteration.

Second, it computes expectations exactly. The targets contain E[ ⋅∣s,a]\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot \mid s,a]E[⋅∣s,a], which the eight-dimensional example already replaced by an average over draws. With a simulator, or with logged data, a target typically uses a single sampled successor. The chapter on sampled Bellman updates studies what this costs: variance, and a bias that comes from maximizing over noisy estimates.

Third, it chooses the states at which targets are computed. Batch reinforcement learning receives a fixed set of transitions instead, and online reinforcement learning a buffer that changes as the agent acts. The error analysis of this chapter said that a fit is controlled only where there are data. The chapter on logged and online data builds the batch algorithms on this template, the tree-based FQI of Ernst et al. (2005) (an averager) and NFQ Riedmiller (2005) (a neural network), runs them on a scheduling log and on ESA’s collision warnings, and then develops DQN, whose design choices respond to the deadly triad.

Fourth, it maximizes over a finite set of actions. Every target contains max⁡a′q(s′,a′;θ)\max_{a'} q(s',a';\theta)maxa′​q(s′,a′;θ). When the action is continuous, a torque or a dose, that maximum is a nonlinear program, to be solved once for every target at every iteration. NFQCA Hafner & Riedmiller (2011) trains a second network, an actor πw(s)≈arg⁡max⁡aq(s,a;θ)\pi_{\boldsymbol w}(s) \approx \arg\max_a q(s,a;\theta)πw​(s)≈argmaxa​q(s,a;θ), and uses it in the target in place of the maximum. The critic qqq is fitted by regression against fixed targets, exactly as in this chapter, and the actor by gradient ascent on the critic. In the terms of Approximate Policy Iteration, NFQCA is approximate policy iteration with one fitted evaluation sweep per improvement, that is, a fitted version of modified policy iteration (Algorithm 4) in which the improvement step is learned as well. The amortized action optimization chapter develops it, together with its online descendants DDPG and TD3. The smooth Bellman operator meets the same obstacle in the partition function over a continuous action set (Continuous Action and State Spaces), and soft actor-critic resolves it in the same way.

State values v(s)v(s)v(s)Action values q(s,a)q(s,a)q(s,a), so acting needs no modelSamples, Logged and online data
Exact expectation in the targetOne sampled successor per transitionSamples
Targets at chosen statesA fixed batch (FQI, NFQ) or a replay buffer (DQN)Logged and online data
Maximum over a finite action setA learned actor in the target (NFQCA, DDPG, TD3)Amortized action optimization

Exercises¶

These exercises complement the shorter ones inside the sections. The first ones are short checks; Exercise 7 reuses the code of the eight-dimensional stopping problem.

Exercise 1 (Weighting shift)

If the fitting distribution puts almost no mass on an important region of the state space, what failure should you expect?

Solution to Exercise 1

The fit may be accurate under the weighted norm yet poor in that neglected region, leading to bad values or decisions there. In the error bound of fitted value iteration, this shows up as a large sup-norm error, or, in the weighted analysis, as a large concentrability coefficient.

Exercise 2 (Accurate fits, bad iteration)

In the two-state counterexample, the function class contains v∗v^*v∗ exactly. Why does fitted value iteration still diverge, and why does Theorem 1 not prevent it?

Solution to Exercise 2

The least-squares fit is not an averager: it stretches the constant target into a line that overshoots at state 2, by a factor 6/56/56/5, which beats the contraction γ\gammaγ when γ>5/6\gamma > 5/6γ>5/6. The fit error at iteration kkk is proportional to θk\theta_kθk​, so there is no single ε\varepsilonε that bounds it for all kkk, and the theorem’s assumption fails.

Exercise 3 (Where the actor enters)

Which part of fitted Q-iteration does the actor of NFQCA replace, and why is it needed only for continuous actions?

Solution to Exercise 3

It replaces the maximization over next actions inside each Bellman target. With a finite action set the maximum is computed by enumeration; with a continuous action set it is a nonlinear program for every target, and the actor amortizes those programs into one trained network.

Exercise 4 (Reading the bounds)

Fitted value iteration with γ=0.9\gamma = 0.9γ=0.9 starts from v0=0v_0 = 0v0​=0, and ∥v∗∥∞=10\|v^*\|_\infty = 10∥v∗∥∞​=10. Every fit is accurate to ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1 in the sup norm.

  1. Bound ∥v50−v∗∥∞\|v_{50} - v^*\|_\infty∥v50​−v∗∥∞​ with Theorem 1, and separate the part that more iterations remove from the part that they do not.

  2. Bound the loss of the greedy policy of v50v_{50}v50​ with Proposition 1.

  3. The duck-harvest table reports policy losses four to five orders of magnitude below the second bound. Name the two places in the proofs where the worst case is charged, and say why neither happens there.

Solution to Exercise 4

  1. ∥v50−v∗∥∞≤0.950⋅10+0.1/0.1=0.052+1\|v_{50} - v^*\|_\infty \le 0.9^{50} \cdot 10 + 0.1/0.1 = 0.052 + 1∥v50​−v∗∥∞​≤0.950⋅10+0.1/0.1=0.052+1. Further iterations shrink the first term only; the second, ε/(1−γ)=1\varepsilon/(1-\gamma) = 1ε/(1−γ)=1, is the price of the fits and stays.

  2. The greedy loss is at most 2γ1−γ⋅1.052≈18.9\tfrac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma} \cdot 1.052 \approx 18.91−γ2γ​⋅1.052≈18.9, nearly twice ∥v∗∥∞\|v^*\|_\infty∥v∗∥∞​, so the bound says nothing useful here.

  3. The value bound charges every fitting error at its worst state and lets the errors add in the same direction at every iteration. The greedy bound charges the worst value error twice, once for each of the two actions being compared. In the duck problem the fitting errors are much smaller than ε\varepsilonε at most states, they do not align over the 50-year horizon, and much of the error is common to all four packages, so it cancels in the comparison that decides the action.

Exercise 5 (Which fits are averagers)

For each fit, say whether it is an averager in the sense of Definition 1, and justify your answer with the weights it puts on the targets.

  1. kkk-nearest neighbors with k=5k = 5k=5 and equal weights.

  2. Kernel regression v^(s)=∑iK(s,si)yi/∑iK(s,si)\hat v(s) = \sum_i K(s, s_i) y_i / \sum_i K(s, s_i)v^(s)=∑i​K(s,si​)yi​/∑i​K(s,si​) with a Gaussian kernel.

  3. Ordinary least squares on the features (1,s)(1, s)(1,s) in one dimension.

  4. A regression tree whose splits are chosen once, from the targets of the first iteration, and then frozen.

  5. A neural network trained to convergence on squared error.

Solution to Exercise 5

  1. Yes: weights 1/51/51/5 on the five nearest training states, zero elsewhere.

  2. Yes: the weights are positive and normalized to sum to one, and they depend only on the states.

  3. No. The prediction at sss is ∑iwi(s)yi\sum_i w_i(s) y_i∑i​wi​(s)yi​ with wi(s)=1m+(s−sˉ)(si−sˉ)/∑j(sj−sˉ)2w_i(s) = \tfrac1m + (s - \bar s)(s_i - \bar s)/\sum_j (s_j - \bar s)^2wi​(s)=m1​+(s−sˉ)(si​−sˉ)/∑j​(sj​−sˉ)2, which is negative for training states on the far side of the mean when sss is far from sˉ\bar ssˉ. The weights do sum to one, so constants are preserved, but monotonicity fails.

  4. Yes, from the iteration at which the splits are frozen: each prediction is the average of the targets in a fixed leaf.

  5. No. The prediction is not a fixed linear function of the targets at all, and nothing constrains its sign or normalization.

Exercise 6 (Fitting the backup or minimizing the residual)

Return to the two-state counterexample: v(1;θ)=θv(1;\theta) = \thetav(1;θ)=θ, v(2;θ)=2θv(2;\theta) = 2\thetav(2;θ)=2θ, every reward zero, state 1 moves to state 2 and state 2 stays put.

  1. Bellman residual minimization chooses θ\thetaθ to minimize ∑s(v(s;θ)−(Lv(⋅;θ))(s))2\sum_s \big(v(s;\theta) - (\Bellman v(\cdot;\theta))(s)\big)^2∑s​(v(s;θ)−(Lv(⋅;θ))(s))2 with equal weights. Write this objective and show that its minimizer is θ=0\theta = 0θ=0 for every γ\gammaγ.

  2. Gradient descent on that objective uses the full gradient. Show that it converges for every γ<1\gamma < 1γ<1 with a small enough step, while fitted value iteration diverges for γ>5/6\gamma > 5/6γ>5/6.

  3. Why is Bellman residual minimization rarely used despite this? Consider what an unbiased estimate of (v(s;θ)−E[r+γv(s′;θ)])2\big(v(s;\theta) - \mathbb{E}[r + \gamma v(s';\theta)]\big)^2(v(s;θ)−E[r+γv(s′;θ)])2 requires when the successor is random, and connect it to the single-sample paradigm of the next chapter.

Solution to Exercise 6

  1. The objective is (θ−2γθ)2+(2θ−2γθ)2=θ2[(1−2γ)2+4(1−γ)2](\theta - 2\gamma\theta)^2 + (2\theta - 2\gamma\theta)^2 = \theta^2\big[(1-2\gamma)^2 + 4(1-\gamma)^2\big](θ−2γθ)2+(2θ−2γθ)2=θ2[(1−2γ)2+4(1−γ)2], a parabola whose coefficient is positive for γ<1\gamma < 1γ<1. Its minimizer is θ=0\theta = 0θ=0.

  2. Gradient descent on a positive-definite quadratic converges for any step size below 2/c2/c2/c, where ccc is its curvature. Fitted value iteration does not descend this objective: it holds the target fixed and fits it, which is the semi-gradient, and the semi-gradient map θ↦65γθ\theta \mapsto \tfrac65\gamma\thetaθ↦56​γθ expands for γ>5/6\gamma > 5/6γ>5/6.

  3. Squaring the residual of a single sampled successor gives E[(v(s)−r−γv(s′))2]\mathbb{E}\big[(v(s) - r - \gamma v(s'))^2\big]E[(v(s)−r−γv(s′))2], which equals the squared residual plus the variance of r+γv(s′)r + \gamma v(s')r+γv(s′). The minimizer is biased toward functions with small variance of the successor value. An unbiased estimate needs two independent successors of the same state, the double-sampling problem, which a log with one successor per transition cannot provide.

Exercise 7 (An averager on the eight-dimensional problem)

In the code of the eight-dimensional stopping problem, add a fit by kkk-nearest neighbors (sklearn.neighbors.KNeighborsRegressor) with k=1k = 1k=1, 10 and 50, and record the largest change max⁡i∣vk+1(si)−vk(si)∣\max_i |v_{k+1}(s_i) - v_k(s_i)|maxi​∣vk+1​(si​)−vk​(si​)∣ at each iteration.

  1. Check that the changes shrink by at least the factor γ=0.9\gamma = 0.9γ=0.9 per iteration, as Theorem 2 guarantees. Do they for the trees and the network?

  2. Compare the mean and largest errors with those of the trees and the network at D=8D = 8D=8. Which value of kkk is best, and why does a large kkk hurt most at the corners of the cube?

Solution to Exercise 7

The changes shrink geometrically, by a factor of about 0.43 to 0.55 per iteration, faster than γ\gammaγ, because the stopping reward caps the values, and they reach 10-14 within the 40 iterations. With k=10k = 10k=10 at D=8D = 8D=8 the mean error is about 0.022 and the largest about 0.155, between the trees (0.031) and the network (0.013) on average. Larger kkk averages targets over a larger neighborhood; at a corner of the cube all neighbors lie on one side, so the prediction is pulled toward the interior, and the largest error grows to about 0.2 at k=50k = 50k=50. For the trees and the network the measurement is worth making, because no theorem predicts its outcome: the splits of the trees depend on the targets, and the network has no sign or normalization constraint.

Exercise 8 (From value iteration to policy iteration, approximately)

Modified policy iteration (Algorithm 4) applies Lπ\BellmanPiLπ​ mmm times after each greedy improvement.

  1. Write fitted modified policy iteration, in which each application of the operator is followed by a fit. Which values of mmm give fitted value iteration and approximate policy iteration?

  2. NFQCA performs one fitted evaluation sweep per improvement, with a learned actor in place of the greedy step. Which mmm is this?

  3. In the exact setting, larger mmm means fewer improvements. Give one reason why a large mmm may be a poor choice when every sweep includes a fit.

Solution to Exercise 8

  1. For j=1,…,mj = 1, \ldots, mj=1,…,m: q←PLπkqq \leftarrow \Proj\mathrm{L}_{\pi_k} qq←PLπk​​q, then πk+1\pi_{k+1}πk+1​ greedy for qqq. With m=1m = 1m=1 each sweep uses the operator of the policy that is greedy for the current values, which is fitted value iteration; m→∞m \to \inftym→∞ is approximate policy iteration with fitted policy evaluation as the evaluation step.

  2. m=1m = 1m=1: NFQCA is the fitted value iteration end of the range, with the maximization in the target done by the actor.

  3. Every fit adds an error, and for a nonlinear fit nothing guarantees that repeated fitted evaluation of a fixed policy converges; with off-policy data it can diverge, which is the deadly triad again. Many sweeps on a policy that is about to change also spend computation on accuracy that the next improvement discards.

Exercise 9 (Designing a convergent fitted iteration)

Pick a problem from an earlier chapter that has a continuous state: the reservoir of the finite-horizon chapter, the storm-surge barrier, or the fishery. Design a fitted value iteration for it that is guaranteed to converge, run it, and compare its greedy policy with the exact one. Then replace the fit by a neural network and report what changes: the number of iterations, the stability of the iterates, and the policy loss. Explain the differences with the results of this chapter.

Solution to Exercise 9

Any averager gives the guarantee: multilinear interpolation on a grid, state aggregation, or kkk-nearest neighbors on sampled states. A report should state the fit, the states where targets are computed, the tolerance, and the policy loss measured against an exact or fine-grid solution. With the network, expect the iterates to wander by an amount comparable to the fit error rather than converge, as in the duck-harvest experiment, and a policy whose errors concentrate where the data are sparse or two actions are close.

Summary and Outlook¶

Replacing the table by a parametric function turns value iteration into fitted value iteration: compute Bellman targets at chosen states, fit the function to them, repeat. Collocation and Galerkin projection are two fitting rules, and regression with trees or neural networks is the one that scales, as the eight-dimensional stopping problem showed. If each fit is accurate to ε\varepsilonε in the sup norm, the value error stays below ε/(1−γ)\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)ε/(1−γ) and the greedy policy loses at most 2γε/(1−γ)22\gamma\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)^22γε/(1−γ)2. On the duck-harvest model both bounds held with one to five orders of magnitude to spare, and the greedy policies were far more accurate than the values. The fit can, however, stretch differences and make the iteration diverge, even when it represents the solution exactly. Averagers cannot, and for policy evaluation, least squares weighted by the stationary distribution of the policy cannot either. Neither argument covers the optimality operator with a neural network, which is the setting of practical fitted Q-iteration. Newton’s method becomes approximate policy iteration, with LSTD and LSPI as its linear case.

Exact target evaluation still assumes access to the transition probabilities or an exact expectation. How can the same Bellman update be estimated when the model supplies only samples? Bellman updates from samples replaces the exact integral by sampled averages and makes their variance and maximization bias explicit.
